label: Dallas

county_election_office.name: Dallas County Elections Department, 1520 Round Table Drive, Dallas 75247

zip_caveats: ZIP codes do not map to Dallas County ballots. For your exact ballot, look up your address at dallascountyvotes.org/voters/ballot. Inside the City of Dallas, these lines all split ZIP codes: six congressional districts on this ballot (CD-5, 6, 24, 30, 32 and 33, redrawn in 2025); 14 Texas House districts (HD-100, 102 to 105, and 107 to 115); State Board of Education Districts 9, 13 and 14; Commissioners Court precincts (only Precincts 2 and 4 elect a commissioner this year, so Precinct 1 and 3 voters see no commissioner race); and justice of the peace and constable Precincts 1 to 5. We list every one of these races because our sources do not show exactly which reach inside city limits; your sample ballot shows only yours. State Senate District 2 is the only Senate seat on the Dallas County ballot this year, and it covers only part of the county. Countywide races (county judge, district attorney, clerks, treasurer, the 298th District Court, every judge in the Uncontested Races box, County Prop A) and the 5th Court of Appeals are on every Dallas County ballot. School districts cross ZIPs too. Most of Dallas is in Dallas ISD, which has nothing on this ballot (its bond passed in May 2026). Part of Dallas is in Mesquite ISD, whose tax rate measure (Mesquite ISD Prop A) appears only for addresses inside that district. Two small parts of West Dallas are in Irving ISD, whose four bond measures (Irving ISD Props A to D) appear only for addresses inside that district. City of Dallas Prop A is only for people who live inside city limits. A Dallas mailing address outside the city does not count, and separate cities surrounded by Dallas such as Highland Park, University Park, Addison and Farmers Branch do not vote on it; several Dallas ZIPs (for example 75205, 75225, 75234 and 75244) include parts of those cities, and some of those ZIPs are left off the list below for that reason. Parts of Dallas lie in Collin and Denton counties (for example parts of 75252 and 75287, which are left off the list below); those residents get a different county ballot that this guide does not cover, though City of Dallas Prop A is on their ballots too. Small parts of the city also sit in Kaufman and Rockwall counties, but the city's November election order names only Dallas, Collin and Denton counties. Measures for Garland, University Park and Wylie also appear on the countywide sample ballot; they are for those cities only. The ZIP list here is a convenience list of ZIPs that are mostly inside the city and in Dallas County, not an official crosswalk.
notes: Dallas County uses vote centers: any registered Dallas County voter can vote at any Dallas County vote center, early or on Election Day. Early voting runs Mon Oct 19 to Fri Oct 30: 7 AM to 7 PM every day except Sunday Oct 25, noon to 6 PM. Election Day, Tue Nov 3, is 7 AM to 7 PM; if you're in line by 7 PM, you can vote. Bring a printed or handwritten cheat sheet into the booth (take it with you when you leave; don't show it to others inside the 100-foot zone). Phones and other devices cannot be used in the voting room. Texas has no straight-ticket voting, so you mark each race one by one, and skipping a race is fine. After the county races, the ballot has an "Uncontested Races" box listing 53 unopposed judges, all Democrats: one choice, "Vote for All" or "Vote for None," covers the whole box. On the ballot, each proposition says "For" or "Against": For means yes, Against means no. There are two different Prop A's: Dallas County Prop A (homelessness tax rate) and City of Dallas Prop A ($443 million public safety bond). They are separate votes. Three local races have a write-in line because a write-in candidate filed: district attorney (Eric Reed), JP Precinct 1, Place 2 (Jayla Godbolt) and U.S. House District 33 (Michelle Craig). To vote for a write-in, you write the name in. A mail ballot can be hand-delivered on Election Day only to the Elections Office at 1520 Round Table Drive while polls are open, by the voter, with photo ID. There is no Dallas mayor or city council race on this ballot.
